title: He Buried the Gods That Never Spoke: The Night Jacob Finally Let Go Before Meeting the God Who Always Did
paragraphs: He Buried the Gods That Never Spoke: The Night Jacob Finally Let Go Before Meeting the God Who Always Did
When God Calls You Back, He Will Confront What You Still Haven’t Buried
There are moments God calls you forward… and you realize you’re still carrying things from a life you were supposed to leave behind.
Jacob knew that feeling.

He had wrestled angels, survived deception, outlived betrayal, and even heard the voice of God. But still… there were things hidden in his camp. Things no one talked about. Things buried in silence long before they were buried in the ground.
And God wasn’t going to let him return to Bethel—the place of encounter—while still holding onto idols.
Genesis 35 opens with a command that sounds simple… but carries the weight of everything Jacob had avoided:
“Then God said to Jacob, ‘Arise, go up to Bethel and dwell there, and make there an altar to God, who appeared to you when you fled from your brother Esau.’”

In Hebrew, the word for “arise” is קוּם (qum)—not just stand up, but rise with intention, awaken, take action that reflects a new direction. This wasn’t just physical movement. It was spiritual confrontation.
Jacob was being called back… but not as the same man.
And deep down, he knew it.
So he turned to his household, his family, his people… and said something that probably shook the entire camp:
“Put away the foreign gods that are among you, purify yourselves, and change your garments.”
The Hebrew phrase for “put away” is הָסִרוּ (hasiru)—to remove, to take away violently if necessary. Not gently. Not gradually. Not “when you feel ready.”
Remove it.
Because idols don’t leave politely.
They cling.
They hide.
They whisper that you still need them.
Some of those idols came from Laban’s house. Some were likely inherited, some secretly kept by Rachel, some quietly tolerated because confronting them would disrupt comfort.
And isn’t that still us?
We say we follow God… but keep certain habits buried in the background.
We worship on Sundays… but cling to control, pride, hidden sin, unforgiveness.
We want Bethel encounters… but refuse Bethel-level surrender.
Jacob understood something in that moment most people avoid their entire lives:
You cannot meet God deeply while secretly serving something else.
So they gave him everything.
Scripture says:
“They gave to Jacob all the foreign gods that they had, and the rings that were in their ears.”
Those earrings weren’t just accessories. In ancient cultures, they were often tied to idol worship, spiritual allegiance, identity markers.
This was deeper than objects.
This was identity being surrendered.
And then… Jacob did something unforgettable.
“He hid them under the oak which was by Shechem.”
The word “hid” in Hebrew is טָמַן (taman)—to bury, to conceal permanently, to remove from sight and access.
Not stored.
Not saved for later.
Buried.
Because what you don’t bury… you will eventually return to.
And here’s what will hit you if you let it…
Jacob didn’t burn them.
He buried them.
Because some things aren’t just destroyed externally… they must be buried internally, where you decide they will never rise again.
There’s something deeply personal about burying.
It means closure.
It means finality.
It means you’ve accepted that part of you is not coming back.
And right there, under that oak near Shechem—a place already marked by past compromise and violence—Jacob made a decision:
The cycle ends here.
No more divided heart.
No more secret attachments.
No more halfway obedience.
And only after that… did God move.
Scripture says a terror from God fell upon the surrounding cities so that no one pursued Jacob’s family.
Do you see it?
Protection followed purification.
Not before.
After.
We often ask God for covering… while still holding onto things He told us to release.
But Jacob’s story reminds us:
Obedience unlocks the protection we keep praying for.
And then he finally arrived at Bethel.
The place where he once slept on a stone, running from his past, unaware of who God really was.
Back then he said, “Surely the Lord is in this place, and I did not know it.”
But now… he knew.
Now he had wrestled.
Now he had lost.
Now he had been renamed.
Now he had buried the idols.
Now Bethel wasn’t just a place of encounter…
It was a place of surrender.
God appeared again and reaffirmed his name:
“Your name is Jacob; no longer shall your name be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name.”
In Hebrew, יִשְׂרָאֵל (Yisra’el) carries the meaning: “one who wrestles with God and prevails.”
But here’s what most people miss:
You don’t prevail by holding on.
You prevail by surrendering.
That’s the scandal of grace.
Jacob, the deceiver…
Jacob, the manipulator…
Jacob, the man who ran…
…became Israel, not because he fixed himself—
but because he finally let go of what was never meant to come with him.
And maybe that’s where this hits you.
You’ve been trying to move forward with God…
But there are still things you haven’t buried.
Still habits.
Still thoughts.
Still attachments.
Still compromises.
Still things you hope God won’t ask about.
But He will.
Not to shame you…
…but to free you.
Because Bethel is waiting.
But idols cannot come with you.
So be honest.
What are you still carrying?
What have you been postponing?
What have you hidden instead of buried?
Be honest. This hit deeper than you expected.
And don’t keep this to yourself.
Because glorifying God isn’t passive.
It’s participation.
It’s obedience.
It’s supporting the work that spreads His truth.
If you’re ready for that kind of growth, that kind of conviction, that kind of transformation…
Because Bethel is not just a place.
It’s the life waiting on the other side of your surrender.
And some things will never change…
until you finally bury them.
